trial_name: ITACTIC — Viscoelastic Haemostatic Assay Augmented Protocols for Major Trauma Haemorrhage (2021)
citation: Baksaas-Aasen K, Gall LS, Stensballe J, et al. Viscoelastic haemostatic assay augmented protocols for major trauma haemorrhage (ITACTIC): a randomized, controlled trial. Intensive Care Med. 2021;47:49-59
trial_type: RCT — investigator-initiated, pragmatic, multicentre, international, parallel-group (1:1), open-label with blinded outcome assessors
one_liner: In adult trauma patients requiring massive hemorrhage protocol activation, VHA-guided goal-directed therapy did not improve 24-hour survival free of massive transfusion compared to CCT-guided therapy.

pico.population: Adult trauma patients with ongoing bleeding requiring local massive hemorrhage protocol activation and RBC transfusion, randomized within 3 hours of injury and within 1 hour of ED admission
pico.intervention: Viscoelastic haemostatic assay (VHA; ROTEM Sigma or TEG 6s) augmented goal-directed protocol plus standard MHP care, with repeated testing every 4 RBC units until haemostasis
pico.comparison: Conventional coagulation test (CCT; PT ratio/INR, fibrinogen, platelet count) augmented goal-directed protocol plus standard MHP care, repeated every 4 RBC units
pico.outcome: Proportion of patients alive and free of massive transfusion (>=10 RBC units) at 24 hours post-injury

background.existing_knowledge: Major trauma hemorrhage is a leading cause of preventable death and is strongly driven by trauma-induced coagulopathy. Contemporary damage control resuscitation improves survival, but conventional plasma-based coagulation tests (PT/INR, fibrinogen, platelets) have turnaround delays during active bleeding.
background.knowledge_gap: Whether adding rapid point-of-care viscoelastic assays (ROTEM/TEG) to guide targeted haemostatic supplementation provides incremental clinical benefit over standardized CCT-guided algorithms in multicenter trauma systems.
background.hypothesis: VHA-guided management enables earlier targeted haemostatic therapy, reduces massive transfusion, and improves survival compared to CCT-guided care.

methods.design: Investigator-initiated, pragmatic, multicentre, international, open-label, parallel-group randomized controlled trial (1:1), stratified by centre using block randomisation
methods.setting: Emergency department trauma resuscitation across 7 European major trauma centres in Denmark, Germany, Norway, Spain, Switzerland, and the UK

inclusion: Clinical signs of active bleeding triggering local massive hemorrhage protocol (MHP) activation
Randomisation within 3 hours of injury and within 1 hour of ED admission
exclusion: No additional exclusion criteria beyond failing inclusion criteria
Patients withdrawing consent post-randomisation were excluded from final analysis

methods.intervention: VHA-guided goal-directed algorithm (ROTEM Sigma or TEG 6s) plus standard MHP care. Baseline and repeat testing after every 4 RBC units until haemostasis. ROTEM triggers: FIBTEM CA5 <10 mm -> 4 g fibrinogen equiv; EXTEM-FIBTEM CA5 diff <30 mm -> 1 pool platelets; EXTEM CA5 >=40 mm and CT >80 s -> 4 units plasma; EXTEM LI30 <85% -> 1 g TXA. RapidTEG triggers: FF-TEG MA <20 mm -> 4 g fibrinogen equiv; RapidTEG-FF MA diff <45 mm -> 1 pool platelets; RapidTEG MA >65 mm and ACT >120 s -> 4 units plasma; LY30 >10% -> 1 g TXA.
methods.comparison: CCT-guided goal-directed algorithm plus standard MHP care. Baseline and repeat testing after every 4 RBC units until haemostasis. CCT triggers: Fibrinogen <2 g/L -> 4 g fibrinogen equiv; platelet count <100x10^9/L -> 1 pool platelets; INR >1.2 with fibrinogen >=2 g/L -> 4 units plasma.
methods.blinding: Open-label to treating clinicians; research personnel collecting safety and outcome data were blinded to allocation.
methods.sample_size_power: 392 patients required to detect an increase in primary outcome from 72% to 85% (80% power, 2-sided alpha 0.05); sample target set to 196 per arm (392 total) to account for 15% post-randomisation attrition.
methods.primary_outcome: Alive and free of massive transfusion (defined as >=10 RBC units within 24 hours post-injury) at 24 hours.
secondary_outcomes: Mortality at 6 hours, 24 hours, 28 days, and 90 days
28-day mortality in severe TBI subgroup (AIS head 4-6)
methods.follow_up: 24 hours for primary endpoint; 28 days and 90 days for survival and functional recovery.

headline_bullets: VHA-guided goal-directed therapy did not improve 24-hour survival free of massive transfusion (67% vs 64%, OR 1.15, p=0.509).
Overall mortality was non-significantly different at 6 hours, 24 hours, 28 days, and 90 days.
VHA guidance increased early pre-haemostasis fibrinogen delivery (median 4 g vs 0 g) without shortening median time to haemostasis (125 vs 122 min).
A prespecified subgroup with severe TBI showed reduced 28-day mortality with VHA (44% vs 74%, p=0.016 for interaction).

outcomes_table.outcome: Alive and free of massive transfusion at 24 h (primary)
outcomes_table.note: Massive transfusion defined as >=10 RBC units within 24 h after injury
Among patients with known cause of death (51 VHA, 56 CCT)
Analysed in 176 VHA and 170 CCT patients
Assessed in patients with available data
Analysed in 198 VHA and 192 CCT patients
Analysed in 198 VHA and 192 CCT patients

safety: Symptomatic thromboembolic events occurred in 17/201 (9%) VHA vs 27/195 (14%) CCT patients (OR 0.57, 95% CI 0.31–1.08, p=0.088).
Multiple organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS) developed in 141/164 (86%) VHA vs 134/159 (84%) CCT patients (OR 1.14, 95% CI 0.62–2.10, p=0.668).
No excess safety signals or adverse event peaks were attributed to VHA-guided haemostatic product delivery.

domains.notes: Central 1:1 allocation using site-stratified block randomisation with opaque sealed envelopes; baseline severity balanced (median ISS 26 vs 26, pre-baseline RBC 2 vs 2 units).
Treating clinicians were unblinded due to testing nature, creating potential performance bias for transfusion decisions; outcome collectors were blinded.

411 randomized; 15 excluded post-consent withdrawal (8 CCT, 7 VHA), leaving ITT n=396 (195 CCT, 201 VHA). Per-protocol was 313/396 (79%) due to 83 exclusions (54 early haemostasis <1h, 16 death <1h, 8 wrong-arm, 5 entry criteria error).

VHA group received more pre-haemostasis study intervention (67% vs 36%), faster time to intervention (61 vs 80 min), and higher pre-haemostasis fibrinogen (4 g vs 0 g median). 24h total RBC (6 vs 6 units) and plasma (6 vs 7 units) were similar. 8 patients received wrong-arm treatment.
Baseline coagulopathy was lower than anticipated (PTr >1.2 in 32% CCT vs 25% VHA). High background adherence to standard care in both arms (pre-baseline TXA 98% vs 94%).

internal_validity.verdict: Moderate internal validity owing to robust randomisation and baseline balance, limited by open-label clinical delivery, lower-than-expected baseline coagulopathy rates, and high per-protocol exclusion rates.

domains.notes: Broad adult trauma cohort triggering massive transfusion protocol and receiving RBCs in major European trauma centres; includes 18–20% severe TBI and baseline shock (median SBP 90–95 mmHg).

Conducted in well-resourced European major trauma centres with established MHP pathways, routine early TXA, and VHA capacity; generalisability may be lower in non-tertiary or resource-constrained settings.

external_validity.verdict: Moderate-to-high external validity for mature, well-resourced trauma systems with established massive hemorrhage pathways and point-of-care testing availability.

strengths: Pragmatic, international, multicentre randomized design across 7 major trauma centres.
Standardised protocolised algorithms in both arms with repeat testing every 4 RBC units.
Primary composite outcome focused on early mortality and transfusion intensity.
High background adherence to contemporary standards including early tranexamic acid.
limitations: Open-label design with clinician-dependent blood product transfusion decisions.
Lower baseline coagulopathy prevalence (25-32%) and event rates than assumed in power calculations.
Minimal separation between arms in total 24-hour RBC and plasma transfusion volumes.
Substantial missing data for 90-day mortality and health status outcomes.
Heterogeneity in VHA testing platforms (ROTEM vs TEG) and fibrinogen products (cryoprecipitate vs concentrate).

critical_appraisal.summary: ITACTIC provides high-quality randomized evidence that routine implementation of VHA-guided algorithms does not improve 24-hour survival free of massive transfusion compared to standard lab-guided algorithms in high-performing trauma systems.
strengths: Rigorous central randomization and allocation concealment
Clear algorithmic standardization across both study arms
High background quality of damage control resuscitation
weaknesses: Trial was underpowered due to lower-than-projected baseline coagulopathy rates
Open-label design creates potential performance bias for transfusion decisions

sections.authors_conclusion: In adult trauma patients with ongoing bleeding managed with massive hemorrhage protocols, VHA-guided goal-directed therapy did not improve the proportion of patients alive and free of massive transfusion at 24 hours compared with CCT-guided therapy.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Replacing standard laboratory-guided MHP algorithms with VHA-guided algorithms does not improve early survival or reduce massive transfusion in mature trauma resuscitation systems.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adult trauma patients with active bleeding triggering massive hemorrhage protocol activation receiving RBC transfusions.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: VHA testing has no clinical value; point-of-care testing may still benefit specific subgroups such as severe traumatic brain injury.
implementation_caveats: VHA infrastructure requires substantial capital, training, and quality assurance investment.
VHA guidance increased early fibrinogen administration without accelerating haemostasis or reducing mortality.
System logistics and speed of product delivery from lab to bedside remain critical determinants of outcome.

controversies.notes: Combining survival and freedom from massive transfusion (<10 RBC units) introduces potential performance bias in an open-label trial where transfusion decisions are clinician-led.
Only 25-32% of patients had baseline PT ratio >1.2, suggesting sample dilution with non-coagulopathic patients unlikely to benefit from assay-guided supplementation.

Secondary analysis showed VHA increased goal-directed treatment probability (76% vs 47%, OR 3.73, p=0.002) and reduced time to treatment (68 vs 110 min, p=0.002), but only 20% achieved coagulopathy correction at 24 hours.
Significant 28-day mortality reduction in severe TBI (44% vs 74%, OR 0.28, p=0.016) is biologically plausible but statistically fragile due to small sample size (n=73) and subgroup multiplicity.

context_related_trials.relation: Recommends early/repeated coagulation monitoring (CCT and/or VHA) and goal-directed therapy (Grade 1B/1C), citing ITACTIC's neutral main trial result while supporting VHA use within structured pathways.

unresolved_questions: Does VHA-guided resuscitation confer a true mortality benefit in targeted cohorts with documented severe coagulopathy or isolated severe TBI?
Can optimizing the sample-to-product delivery chain improve clinical outcomes independently of the coagulation assay platform used?

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: VHA-guided resuscitation algorithms do not improve survival free of massive transfusion compared to standard laboratory-guided care in major trauma hemorrhage.
